news.title: Springville Once Supplied Iron Ore to Three States
news.summary: An 1880 census records a St. Clair County mine near Springville producing 12,085 tons of iron ore. Where did the ore go, why did mining decline, and could some of that iron have returned as the cast-iron storefront on Main Street?
body: I wonder whether the iron columns on the old Presley Store at 601 Main Street might contain iron mined from the hills around Springville. I do not know, but the timing is interesting. Years before the store was built in 1902, Springville was sending ore to iron furnaces in Alabama, Tennessee and Georgia.

When the Alabama and Chattanooga Railroad reached Springville in 1870, local businessmen could finally move large quantities of ore to customers outside the area. The cost of hauling that much rock by wagon over long distances would have limited the market considerably.

By 1877, A. W. Woodall was mining in the Springville area. By 1880, he was selling ore to James W. Sloss and Henry DeBardeleben, two of the men who helped build Birmingham’s iron industry. Around 1900, Woodall built an ore tram across Talladega Street. I would be interested to see a photograph of that stretch of road from those years.

David A. Aderholt was one of the pioneers of Springville’s iron ore trade with Tennessee. He was a merchant and real estate dealer, served as mayor from 1878 to 1885 and later helped organize Spring Lake College. His 1904 biography credits him with developing the ore trade in this part of Alabama. I find it interesting that one of the men who helped build Springville’s economy also helped establish its college.

The 1880 census records Hugh Carlisle’s St. Clair County operation at 12,085 short tons of iron ore, placing it sixth among the 29 Alabama mining operations listed on that census page. The directory calls the location ‘Near Springfield,’ but an 1889 report in The Iron Age places Carlisle’s mining operation near Springville. The comparison is for individual mines, not the total production of each town.

Carlisle sold ore to the Southern States Coal, Iron and Land Company and to the furnace at Rising Fawn, Georgia, according to the census. The Rising Fawn operation lists stoves, machinery, bar iron and nails among its uses for iron.

Ore was smelted to produce pig iron, which could then be refined or melted down to make other goods. South Pittsburg, Tennessee, eventually became the home of Lodge Cast Iron. Springville ore was shipped to that town, which makes me curious about the origins of the iron used in its cookware. I have not found a record connecting the two.

The 1880 census mining survey gives land descriptions for several mines and prospects, including two Woodall properties and an Aderholt mine four miles northeast of town. Figure 159 shows the soft red ore changing to harder bluish limestone below a fault. The survey lists the landowner as A. D. Aderholt.

One sample from Woodall’s property contained 53.28% metallic iron and another contained 49.49%. The survey tested ore from Aderholt’s stockpile beside the railroad at 48.40%. There was good reason for manufacturers to be interested in these deposits.

The 1910 geological survey describes a prospect 2½ miles northwest of Springville and more workings along the ridge northeast of town. At one site 1½ miles north of the old St. Clair railroad switch, miners reportedly took out 12,000–15,000 tons in about two years. Some underground passages extended 50–200 feet.
These township and section numbers should help locate the mines on modern property maps. Identifying the present landowners and mineral-rights holders would be an interesting next step.

What surprised me most was a report in The Iron Age dated February 7, 1889. The writer described Carlisle’s former mining operation near Springville, noted the quantity and quality of the available ore and then said that ‘no work is now done there.’ Woodall’s later tram indicates that mining activity in the area did not necessarily end with Carlisle’s operation.

Even in 1910, federal geologists considered the ridge northeast of Springville a possible source of iron ore. They also described folds, steeply angled beds and a nearby fault. Following a vein underground could be a good deal more difficult than finding ore exposed at the surface.

I suspect the growth of Birmingham’s iron industry had much to do with the decline of mining in Springville. Consider how much more ore a miner might recover along a 21-foot seam than a 3- or 4-foot bed. Birmingham’s large furnace companies also controlled mines, coal supplies and transportation close to their plants. Smaller operations shipping ore from another town faced considerable competition. The exact date of Springville’s last ore shipment remains an open question.

Other businesses were developing in Springville during the same years. Goodwin’s Mill was grinding grain along Canoe Creek around 1900, and Bob Ewing established a cotton gin in 1902. The stores and bank downtown served farmers throughout the surrounding area. The dates suggest that farming, milling and trade grew alongside the ore business rather than taking its place all at once.

The Presley brothers’ general store was built in 1902. Its cast-iron storefront is unusual in St. Clair County. The 1982 National Register nomination does not name the builder or architect, nor does it identify the foundry responsible for the ironwork.

I like the possibility that some ore taken from a Springville mine left town on a railroad car and came back years later as part of the Presley Store. I have no evidence that this happened. The columns may have been cast from iron mined elsewhere, recycled scrap or a mixture of materials.

A manufacturer’s mark on one of the columns or an old invoice from the Presley family might help identify the foundry, although tracing the iron back to a particular mine would be more difficult. If you know where Woodall’s tram crossed Talladega Street, have photographs of the mining operations or know something about the Presley Store’s ironwork, I would love to hear from you.

news.title: Springville Once Attracted Visitors With Giant Carp
news.summary: Mayor James McLaughlin stocked Springville’s former lake with carp that grew large enough to become a local attraction. By the 1950s, families traveling through town were stopping to feed the fish by hand.
body: Jerry C. Smith recalls feeding the fish during childhood trips in this illustrated account of Springville Lake.

news.title: Springville Once Had Its Own College
news.summary: Spring Lake College once drew students to Springville from as far away as Texas. Some boarded with local families in the early 1900s.
body: Discover St. Clair explores the college and the town's history through the recollections of local residents.

news.title: Springville Has St. Clair County's Only Cast-Iron Storefront
news.summary: Did you know the Presley Store at 601 Main Street has the only cast-iron storefront in St. Clair County? Built in 1902 for brothers Porter and John Presley, it's a one-of-a-kind part of downtown Springville.
body: Explore the Presley Store's history and photograph on Wikipedia.

news.title: Summer Readers Grow More Than 3,200%
news.summary: When Jamie Twente arrived in 2015, Springville Public Library's previous summer reading record was just 25. In 2026, participation reached 829—more than 3,200% above that earlier mark. A remarkable achievement for Twente and the library team.
body: Read The Trussville Tribune's original report for the story behind the library's success.

news.title: Springville's downtown is a nationally recognized historic district
news.summary: Springville's historic district joined the National Register of Historic Places on July 3, 1997, recognizing the architecture and history of its old downtown.
body: Did you know Springville has a historic district recognized by the National Park Service? The Springville Historic District was added to the National Register of Historic Places on July 3, 1997.

The federal listing identifies architecture, commerce and social history as reasons the area matters. Its documented architectural styles include Late Victorian, Queen Anne and Early Commercial, reflecting how Springville developed as a railroad-era trading town.

The district covers part of the historic downtown around streets such as Academy, Wilson and Cross. The recognition helps tell the story of buildings and neighborhoods residents still encounter today.
news.sourceName: National Park Service · National Register of Historic Places

news.title: The night a train explosion shook Springville
news.shortTitle: A Train Derailment Set Off Explosions
news.summary: On January 16, 1969, a train derailed at the Springville Depot. Its cars struck propane tanks, setting off explosions and a fire.
body: On January 16, 1969, a train derailed at the Springville Depot. Its cars struck propane tanks, setting off explosions and a fire.
Firefighters came from as far away as Birmingham, and the National Guard joined the response. Buildings were damaged, but no one was killed.

news.title: When Springville was Pinkhill
news.summary: For a brief time in the 1830s, a letter bound for what is now Springville could be addressed to Pinkhill.
body: The settlement’s earlier name was Big Springs. Fresh water made it a stopping place for Native Americans and, later, settlers traveling through the area. When the first post office opened in 1833, the name on the mail was Pinkhill.

Pinkhill had a short run. In December 1834 the name changed to Springville, bringing the springs back into the town’s name. Of the town’s three names, two point to the water that first drew people here.

news.title: Springville's Charlie Hare signs with Gadsden State
news.summary: Springville High School senior Charlie Hare signed to play baseball for Gadsden State, with one more season ahead for the Tigers.
body: Springville High School center fielder Charlie Hare signed his letter of intent on Nov. 12 to play college baseball for the Gadsden State Cardinals, according to a Nov. 17 report in The Trussville Tribune.
Hare's junior season was cut short by injury. Before then he was batting .375 with a .460 on-base percentage. He plans to return for one more Tigers season, expected to begin in March.

news.title: New Springville art gallery planned for Highway 11
news.summary: Dibble Dabble Art Gallery announced a Nov. 12 opening at 6441 U.S. Highway 11, with art by local and central Alabama artists.
body: Dibble Dabble Art Gallery announced a grand opening and ribbon cutting for Nov. 12 at 6441 U.S. Highway 11 in Springville, according to a Nov. 11 report by The Trussville Tribune.

The opening-day schedule included a glassblowing event and an evening open house. The gallery was described as a place to see work by local and central Alabama artists. Check with the gallery directly for current visiting hours.
